sets.title: Kolam at the Doorstep
sets.text: Every morning before sunrise, millions of women across Tamil Nadu bend over their thresholds and draw kolams, intricate patterns made of rice flour. The practice looks decorative, but it carries several purposes. Rice flour feeds ants and small birds, so the drawing is an act of daily charity to other creatures. The geometry, built on a grid of dots, is also a mental exercise that grandmothers pass on to granddaughters. In recent years, apartment living and the convenience of printed stickers have led many families to abandon the habit. Some folklorists lament this, but others argue that the tradition is simply changing form: colourful kolam competitions in Chennai during the Margazhi month now draw thousands of entrants, and a few mathematicians have begun studying the patterns for their symmetry. Whether stickers or flour, the underlying idea of beginning the day with a small, careful act of creation seems unlikely to vanish altogether.

sets.title: The Millet Revival
sets.text: For decades, ragi, bajra and jowar were treated as the food of the poor in India, while polished rice and wheat, distributed through the public system, became the aspirational staples. The result was a quiet nutritional cost: millets, rich in fibre, iron and calcium, disappeared from many plates, even as diabetes rates climbed. Then the tide turned. After the government declared a year dedicated to millets, restaurants in Bengaluru began serving ragi dosas and foxtail-millet biryani, and start-ups introduced millet cookies and breakfast mixes. Farmers in dryland districts, who had shifted to water-hungry crops, are returning to millets because the grains need little irrigation. Critics warn, however, that fashionable pricing could put millets beyond the reach of the very communities that once depended on them. If urban demand pushes prices up without raising farmers' share, the revival may enrich retailers more than growers. A genuine revival, therefore, must reach the village kitchen and the field, not just the menu of a cafe.

sets.title: Mumbai's Dabbawalas
sets.text: Every working day, about two thousand men in white caps carry nearly two lakh lunchboxes across Mumbai, collecting them from suburban homes in the morning and returning the empties by evening. The system uses no computers. Each box carries a code of letters, numbers and colours painted on its lid, which tells the next carrier at every railway station where it must go. A box may pass through four or five hands, yet errors are reported to be extremely rare. Management scholars who studied the service were struck by its discipline rather than its technology: carriers are shareholders in their own cooperative, so mistakes cost them directly, and the group has met its deadlines for over a century without formal training in logistics. Some visitors expect the carriers to adopt mobile apps, but the dabbawalas themselves see little reason to change something that works. What they have adopted, quietly, is an online booking facility for customers, which handles requests while leaving the delivery chain untouched.

sets.title: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs
sets.text: When Indian Railways began withdrawing some overnight passenger trains from its schedules to speed up express services, the decision looked sensible on a spreadsheet. The slow trains lost money, blocked tracks and carried few passengers per coach. Yet in the districts they served, the effect was immediate. Vegetable sellers who rode the 4 a.m. local to reach city markets could no longer arrive before the morning rush; students from nearby villages missed the early shift at polytechnics; and daily-wage workers faced a bus fare several times the train ticket. Railway officials point out that buses and shared autos fill the gap, and that faster trains benefit far more people overall. This may be true in total, but averages conceal who bears the cost. A transport policy judged only by the speed of the best train neglects the passengers for whom a slow train was the only affordable option. Efficiency measured in minutes saved should be weighed against the livelihoods it quietly removes.

sets.title: Houseboats and the Backwaters
sets.text: Alappuzha's backwaters draw lakhs of visitors each year, and houseboats have become the symbol of Kerala tourism. Over the last decade, the number of boats has grown from a few hundred to well over a thousand. Owners earn good money in the peak months, and hundreds of cooks, boatmen and guides depend on them. But the canals are not wide, and the weight of motor traffic has begun to show. Waste from some boats flows directly into the water, fish stocks near popular routes have thinned, and fishermen complain that their nets are torn by passing hulls. The Vembanad lake, which receives much of the discharge, has seen a rise in algal growth. The state has responded with a licensing cap and mandatory waste tanks, though enforcement is uneven. Environmentalists argue that a smaller number of better-run boats would earn almost as much while protecting the water, since visitors pay for calm, clean scenery rather than crowded canals. Tourism that destroys the very scenery it sells cannot last.

sets.title: Small-Town Cricket
sets.text: In small towns across India, the path to professional cricket used to run through a single local coach with a bucket of worn balls and an uneven pitch. Talent was noticed by chance, often when a visiting selector happened to see a boy bowl. Today the picture is changing. District associations run trials with video analysis, and academies in towns such as Hubballi and Tirunelveli use bowling machines and fitness tests once confined to metros. The effect is visible in the national sides, which increasingly include players from places that were once cricketing backwaters. Yet the gains are uneven. Academy fees remain high, and a gifted boy whose family cannot afford them may still be overlooked. Scholarships offered by some state bodies help, but they cover only a fraction of those who apply. Until selection depends less on what a family can pay and more on what a player can do, the democratisation of Indian cricket will remain half-finished.

sets.title: Reading the Monsoon Forecast
sets.text: The India Meteorological Department issues its first monsoon forecast in April, and farmers, bankers and policymakers wait for it with equal anxiety. Yet the forecast is a probability, not a promise. A prediction of a 'normal' season means total rainfall between 96 and 104 per cent of the long-period average, but that figure says nothing about distribution. A district may receive its entire quota in two violent weeks, flooding the fields, and then stay dry for a month in the sowing window. For a farmer, such a season is a failure even though the national total is normal. Newer models that combine ocean temperatures, satellite data and local weather stations have improved short-range forecasts, and SMS alerts now reach millions of farmers about when rain is likely in their block. Still, scientists caution that long-range prediction will remain approximate, because the monsoon depends on interactions between the sea and atmosphere that are not fully understood. Users of forecasts, therefore, do well to treat them as guidance and keep contingency plans ready.

sets.title: Ikat at Pochampally
sets.text: In Pochampally, a town in Telangana, weavers tie and dye threads in patterns before they ever reach the loom, a technique called ikat. The pattern is fixed in the yarn, so the weaver must align each thread exactly; a slip of a few millimetres blurs the design. A single saree may take a week or more. Power looms elsewhere now print similar-looking designs on cloth in minutes and sell them at a fraction of the price, and many buyers cannot tell the difference at a glance. The weavers' response has been less to compete on price than to prove authenticity: the town's cloth carries a geographical indication tag, and cooperatives train younger members to market directly through online stores. Several young designers have also begun using ikat in jackets and home furnishing, widening the market beyond sarees. It is an encouraging sign that a craft thought to be fading is being rescued not by sentiment but by thoughtful adaptation.

sets.title: UPI and Everyone Else
sets.text: Within a few years, the Unified Payments Interface changed how Indians pay for tea, vegetables and auto rides. A flower seller in Madurai displays a printed QR code beside her baskets, and customers pay without exchanging change. The system succeeded partly because it was free for most users and worked across banks, so no one was locked into a single provider. But the same convenience raises a quiet worry. Small shopkeepers say that when networks fail in the middle of a rush, they lose sales, since many customers no longer carry cash. Older users, who are not comfortable with smartphones, rely on grandchildren to complete payments, and are therefore less in control of their own money. Banking experts suggest that cash should remain available as a fallback, and that simple voice-based options be designed for the elderly. A payment system truly serves everyone only when it keeps working for those with the weakest connection and the least confidence.

sets.title: The Living Wall of Sundarbans
sets.text: The mangrove forests of the Sundarbans act as a living wall between the Bay of Bengal and the villages behind it. Their tangled roots slow cyclone surges, trap silt and shelter fish nurseries that feed thousands of families. When Cyclone Amphan struck in 2020, villages shielded by dense mangroves suffered far less damage than those where the trees had been cleared for shrimp ponds. Yet clearing continues because shrimp farming pays quickly, while the benefits of mangroves arrive slowly and are shared by everyone. Rising sea levels are also swallowing islands such as Ghoramara, forcing families to move inland. Conservation groups encourage villagers to plant mangrove saplings and offer them paid work for it, an approach that treats local residents as partners rather than offenders. The strategy depends on money, though, and funds are usually the first thing cut when budgets tighten. If planting is abandoned, the sea will be quick to reclaim what the villagers had begun to restore.

sets.title: More Than Quiet Rooms
sets.text: Public libraries in Indian cities have long been dismissed as quiet rooms for retired men to read newspapers. A few are proving otherwise. In Kozhikode, a district library now keeps its doors open until late in the evening and runs weekend clubs where children from nearby slums learn to code on shared computers. A Pune library offers a quiet corner for students who have no space to study at home, and its reading room is filled by six every morning. Librarians report that the number of young members has doubled since such services began. What attracts them is rarely the books alone; it is the feeling of a safe, free place to belong. Some officials still view libraries as a luxury, to be trimmed when money is short. That view mistakes their purpose. A library that opens opportunities for those without them does more for a city than another flyover, and it costs a fraction as much.

sets.title: What the Metro Taught Us
sets.text: When the Delhi Metro opened its first line in 2002, many predicted that Indians would never queue, never keep stations clean and never give up their seats. Two decades later, those predictions look wrong. Commuters line up behind painted markers, security checks are routine, and coaches reserved for women are broadly respected. Planners credit this less to any special civic virtue than to design: clear signs, frequent trains, and fines that are consistently enforced. People behave well when good behaviour is easy and bad behaviour is reliably penalised. The same lesson has been applied in newer systems in Kochi and Lucknow, where stations were planned with wide stairways to reduce crowding at peak hours. Critics note that the Metro serves mainly the middle class and that last-mile connectivity from stations remains poor. These are fair complaints, but they concern the reach of the system, not its demonstration that public behaviour can change when the system around it is well built.

sets.title: Chennai and Chess
sets.text: Chennai has become something of a chess capital in India, and the reason lies partly in its neighbourhoods. In many streets, a boy or girl learns the game from an uncle on the verandah long before joining a formal academy. Coaches in the city started offering group classes in schools and later moved online, so that a talented child in a small town can face strong opponents at home. The state government encouraged this by hosting an international tournament and by funding a few young prodigies. Results followed: several teenagers from the city have earned grandmaster titles, and India's teams have begun to challenge traditional powers. Observers caution, however, that early success invites pressure. Children who begin tournament play at six or seven often burn out by fifteen, and the pursuit of ratings can crowd out schooling. Parents and coaches need to remember that the game's joy is meant to sustain a player, not merely the title.

sets.title: The Village That Runs on the Sun
sets.text: Modhera in Gujarat, famous for its eleventh-century Sun Temple, was declared India's first fully solar-powered village in 2022. Rooftop panels on homes and public buildings, together with a ground-mounted plant, supply electricity during the day, and batteries store the surplus for use after sunset. Households have seen their power bills fall sharply, and some now sell extra power back to the grid. The village's transformation matters less for its scale, which is small, than for what it shows. A community with a tradition of sun worship has become a testing ground for sun-based energy; local people, not outside engineers, operate and maintain the equipment. Larger towns will find it harder, because rooftops are crowded and ownership is divided among many tenants and landlords. Even so, Modhera answers a common objection, that renewable energy is suited only to technical experts. If a farming community can manage it, a housing society in a city may well be able to as well.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage on kolams? (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)
options: Kolam serves several purposes and, though under pressure from modern living, continues in changing forms.
Kolam survives today only because of competitions held in Chennai.
Printed stickers have completely replaced the kolam in Tamil Nadu homes.
Kolam patterns are valuable mainly as material for mathematical research.
questions.explanation: The passage lists the purposes of kolam, notes its decline in apartments, then shows new forms (contests, study) keeping it alive. Only the first option covers all of this; the others each seize on one detail.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred about how the kolam tradition has been handed down? (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)
options: It has been taught chiefly in schools through printed manuals.
It has been passed on largely through informal teaching within families.
It has been restricted to boys of priestly families.
It has been transmitted only through public competitions.
questions.explanation: The passage says grandmothers pass the geometry to granddaughters, which points to family-based, informal transmission. Nothing mentions schools, manuals or restricting it to boys.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'lament' (in 'Some folklorists lament this') most nearly means (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)
options: celebrate loudly
take no notice of
express sorrow over
question the origin of
questions.explanation: The folklorists are contrasted with those who say the tradition is merely changing, so they regret the abandonment. 'Lament' means to mourn or regret.
questions.shortcut: Contrast word 'but others argue' tells you the first group is unhappy.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the future of the kolam tradition is best described as (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)
options: bitterly nostalgic
dismissive
deeply alarmed
cautiously optimistic
questions.explanation: The author admits decline but cites contests and research, and ends by saying the underlying idea 'seems unlikely to vanish'. That is hopeful but hedged ('seems').

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is a matter of verifiable fact rather than opinion or prediction? (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)
options: Kolams are drawn with rice flour, which feeds ants and small birds.
The kolam tradition is simply changing form rather than dying out.
The habit of starting the day with a small act of creation will not vanish.
Printed stickers are a poorer substitute for hand-drawn patterns.
questions.explanation: That kolams are made of rice flour that feeds ants and birds can be checked. The 'changing form' claim is an interpretation, the 'will not vanish' claim is a prediction, and the sticker claim is a value judgement.

questions.questionText: The main point of the passage is that (Passage: The Millet Revival)
options: millets are nutritionally inferior to rice and wheat but are now fashionable.
the revival of millets is welcome, but it will be genuine only if it benefits farmers and poorer consumers.
restaurants and start-ups are the only groups gaining from the millet revival.
the government should stop distributing rice and wheat through the public system.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the decline, the revival, then a warning that benefits must reach villages and growers. The first option joins the welcome and the caution; the rest distort or invent claims.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be reasonably inferred from the passage? (Passage: The Millet Revival)
options: Millets contain less fibre than polished rice.
Dryland farmers had never grown millets before.
Government channels made rice and wheat far more available to ordinary households than millets.
Diabetes in India is caused only by the disappearance of millets.
questions.explanation: Rice and wheat were 'distributed through the public system' and became the staples, implying wider access. The passage says millets are rich in fibre, and it never says farmers never grew them or that millets alone cause diabetes.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, 'aspirational' (staples) means (Passage: The Millet Revival)
options: difficult to digest
grown only in cities
cheap and quickly spoiled
associated with higher status and desired by many
questions.explanation: Rice and wheat were set against millets, 'the food of the poor', so they were the foods people wished to move up to. 'Aspirational' means that which people aspire to.
questions.shortcut: Look at the contrast: poor man's food versus the aspirational one.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards the millet revival is best described as (Passage: The Millet Revival)
options: approving but cautious
enthusiastic without any reservation
sceptical and dismissive
indifferent and detached
questions.explanation: The author welcomes the revival (farmers return, nutrition) yet warns about pricing and who profits. That mix is approving but cautious.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements from the passage is an opinion? (Passage: The Millet Revival)
options: Restaurants in Bengaluru began serving ragi dosas and foxtail-millet biryani.
A genuine revival must reach the village kitchen and the field, not just the cafe menu.
Millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium.
Farmers in dryland districts are returning to millets.
questions.explanation: The three other statements report events or properties that can be verified. 'Must reach the village kitchen' states what the author thinks ought to happen, a normative judgement.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred about the very low error rate of the dabbawalas? (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)
options: It is mainly due to GPS tracking fitted to each lunchbox.
It results from formal degrees in logistics held by the carriers.
It is linked to the carriers bearing the cost of mistakes as part-owners of the cooperative.
It is achieved because customers pay extra for error insurance.
questions.explanation: The passage says carriers are shareholders so 'mistakes cost them directly', and also says there is no computer system or formal logistics training. So ownership-driven care is the supported inference.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'struck by' (in 'were struck by its discipline') most nearly means (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)
options: hit physically by
irritated by
puzzled by
impressed by
questions.explanation: The scholars studied the service and noted what stood out as its discipline, which is a positive reaction. 'Struck by' here means strongly impressed.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage towards the dabbawala system is best described as (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)
options: admiring
mocking
apprehensive
resentful
questions.explanation: The author stresses no computers, century-long punctuality and rare errors, all of which are praised. The tone is admiring, with no mockery or fear.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact stated in the passage, rather than an opinion? (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)
options: The dabbawalas should adopt mobile apps for delivery.
Each lunchbox carries a code of letters, numbers and colours on its lid.
Discipline is more admirable than any technology.
Mumbai's lunchbox delivery is the best logistics system in the world.
questions.explanation: The code on the lid is a physical, checkable detail given in the passage. The other three options express judgements or recommendations that the passage does not establish as facts.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage? (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)
options: Mobile Apps Transform Mumbai's Deliveries
The Decline of Suburban Railways
Lunchboxes Without Computers: The Dabbawalas of Mumbai
A Manual of Logistics for Managers
questions.explanation: The passage is about a delivery service that works without computers through discipline and cooperative ownership. The first title captures both subject and point; the others are off-topic or contradict the text.

questions.questionText: The central argument of the passage is that (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)
options: express trains are less useful than slow passenger trains.
buses and shared autos fully replace the withdrawn trains.
Indian Railways should stop running any loss-making services.
efficiency-based withdrawal of slow trains harms poorer commuters, and policy should weigh such costs.
questions.explanation: The author concedes the spreadsheet logic, then shows who loses and ends by asking for livelihoods to be weighed. Option one captures that; option two and three contradict the author.

questions.questionText: The word 'conceal' in 'averages conceal who bears the cost' most nearly means (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)
options: hide
reveal
calculate
improve
questions.explanation: An average combines everyone's outcomes, so it makes it hard to see who is losing. 'Conceal' means to hide from view.
questions.shortcut: Opposite of 'reveal' - the sentence says averages do not show the burden.

questions.questionText: The author's tone in discussing the railway decision is best described as (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)
options: hostile and sarcastic
critical but measured
wholly approving
detached and indifferent
questions.explanation: The author grants that officials' claim 'may be true in total' but argues the policy neglects the poor. That is criticism expressed in a reasoned, restrained way.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements from the passage is an opinion? (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)
options: Vegetable sellers rode the 4 a.m. local to reach city markets.
The withdrawn slow trains carried few passengers per coach.
Efficiency measured in minutes saved should be weighed against the livelihoods it quietly removes.
Railway officials say buses and shared autos fill the gap.
questions.explanation: The other three report conditions or statements that can be checked. 'Should be weighed' expresses what the author believes is right, which makes it an opinion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage? (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)
options: Why Express Trains Deserve More Funding
The History of the 4 a.m. Local
Comparing Bus and Train Fares in Districts
When Speed Leaves the Poor Behind
questions.explanation: The passage's point is that faster-train policy imposes hidden costs on people who depended on slow trains. The first title states that; the second reverses the argument and the others are minor details.

questions.questionText: The passage mainly argues that (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)
options: the rapid growth of houseboats is harming the backwaters and needs firmer limits and better management.
houseboat tourism should be stopped completely in Kerala.
fishermen are the main cause of pollution in Vembanad lake.
Alappuzha's tourism earns too little to support local workers.
questions.explanation: After describing the boom, the passage lists environmental damage, the partial official response, and the call for fewer, better-run boats. It does not call for a complete ban, blame fishermen, or say earnings are low.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred about the measures taken by the state? (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)
options: They have stopped the growth of houseboats entirely.
They have not fully solved the pollution problem because enforcement is uneven.
They have made fishermen satisfied with the canals.
They have caused houseboat owners to lose all their income.
questions.explanation: The passage says the licensing cap and waste tanks exist 'though enforcement is uneven', and damage is still described. So the problem persists in part. The other options are unsupported.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the present state of houseboat tourism is best described as (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)
options: celebratory
indifferent
concerned and cautionary
hostile to tourism of any kind
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges benefits but spends most of the passage on damage and ends with a warning. That is concern, not celebration; and the support for 'better-run boats' shows no opposition to all tourism.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)
options: The number of houseboats has grown from a few hundred to well over a thousand.
Fishermen complain that passing hulls tear their nets.
The state has introduced a licensing cap and mandatory waste tanks.
Tourism that destroys the very scenery it sells cannot last.
questions.explanation: The other statements report numbers, complaints, or official actions. The final one is a general judgement or prediction about sustainability that cannot be verified as a fact.

questions.questionText: The most suitable title for the passage is (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)
options: Tourism Boom, Backwater Burden
How to Book a Houseboat in Alappuzha
Kerala's Finest Fishing Spots
The Ancient History of Vembanad Lake
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the growth in houseboat tourism with its burden on the backwaters. The first title conveys that tension; the others cover topics the passage does not discuss.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage? (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)
options: Metro academies remain far superior to those in small towns.
Small-town cricket has gained better facilities and visibility, but cost still limits who benefits.
Scholarships have solved the problem of unequal access to cricket.
National selectors now choose players only from backward towns.
questions.explanation: The passage traces improvement (trials, academies, national representation) and then the remaining barrier of fees. The first option holds both; the others misstate the text.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that earlier, the discovery of cricketing talent in small towns (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)
options: was handled by well-funded district academies.
was done through video analysis of every boy.
depended largely on chance.
was impossible for anyone without a scholarship.
questions.explanation: The passage says that earlier 'talent was noticed by chance', as when a visiting selector happened to watch a boy bowl. Academies and video analysis are described as recent changes.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'democratisation' most nearly means (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)
options: introducing elections in cricket bodies
growing the commercial value of cricket
reducing the number of players selected
making opportunity accessible to people of all backgrounds
questions.explanation: The sentence concerns selection depending less on family wealth and more on ability. So the word refers to opening access to all, regardless of means.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion expressed in the passage? (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)
options: Until selection depends less on a family's means, democratisation of Indian cricket will remain half-finished.
District associations run trials with video analysis.
Scholarships from some state bodies cover only a fraction of applicants.
Academies in Hubballi and Tirunelveli use bowling machines.
questions.explanation: The three other options are reported practices that can be checked. 'Half-finished' is an evaluation of progress and so is a matter of judgement.

questions.questionText: The passage would be best titled (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)
options: The Coach with a Bucket of Balls
Small-Town Cricket's Rise, Held Back by Cost
Why Metros Dominate Indian Cricket
Bowling Machines and Their Price
questions.explanation: The passage is about improvement in small-town cricket and the remaining obstacle of fees. The first title covers both parts; the others pick a detail or reverse the point.

questions.questionText: The passage chiefly conveys that (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)
options: monsoon forecasts are so unreliable that they should be ignored.
the monsoon can now be predicted exactly for every district.
monsoon forecasts are useful but probabilistic, so users should plan for uncertainty.
normal rainfall always guarantees a good harvest.
questions.explanation: The passage explains what 'normal' means, how distribution can fail farmers, how short-range forecasts have improved, and concludes that forecasts are guidance. Only the first option fits.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)
options: The April forecast of the IMD is usually wrong.
SMS alerts have made long-range forecasting exact.
Floods cannot occur in a season of normal total rainfall.
A forecast of a normal season does not guarantee a good season for every farmer.
questions.explanation: The passage gives the example of a district getting its quota in two weeks and then going dry in the sowing window, even when the national total is normal. It does not say April forecasts are usually wrong or that floods cannot occur.
questions.shortcut: Look for the example in the passage that the option generalises.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, 'contingency plans' are (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)
options: backup plans for unexpected situations
permanent long-term plans
plans to invest in banks
legal contracts with insurers
questions.explanation: Since forecasts are only guidance, users should have alternatives ready if the season goes differently. That is what a contingency plan is - preparation for events that may happen.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion or recommendation, not a fact? (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)
options: The IMD issues its first monsoon forecast in April.
Users of forecasts do well to treat them as guidance.
A 'normal' season means rainfall between 96 and 104 per cent of the long-period average.
SMS alerts now reach millions of farmers.
questions.explanation: The other statements can be checked against records. 'Do well to treat them as guidance' is advice and so is a judgement.

questions.questionText: The most appropriate title for the passage is (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)
options: Why Rainfall Totals Never Matter
The Satellites That Control the Monsoon
Reading the Monsoon Forecast: Guidance, Not a Guarantee
How Bankers Decide Farm Loans
questions.explanation: The passage's theme is how to understand and use monsoon forecasts, which are probabilistic. The first title says this; the others are unsupported or marginal.

questions.questionText: The main idea of the passage is that (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)
options: power looms have made ikat weaving obsolete in Telangana.
ikat can be woven quickly if the threads are dyed in advance.
designers should abandon sarees and make only jackets.
Pochampally weavers are sustaining their craft through authenticity, direct marketing and new products despite cheap imitations.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the labour of ikat, the threat from printed imitations, and three responses (GI tag, online sales, new products). The first option sums this up.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)
options: The geographical indication tag helps buyers tell genuine Pochampally cloth from lookalikes.
Power-loom cloth is of higher quality than ikat.
Young weavers have refused to sell online.
Ikat can be used only for sarees.
questions.explanation: The weavers 'prove authenticity' with the tag because many buyers cannot tell cloth apart at a glance. The passage also says ikat is now used for jackets and furnishings and that cooperatives train younger members to sell online.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'authenticity' most nearly means (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)
options: popularity among buyers
the quality of being genuine
low cost of production
great antiquity
questions.explanation: Weavers are responding to cheap look-alikes by proving that their cloth is the real thing. 'Authenticity' means genuineness.

questions.questionText: The author's tone in the closing sentence is best described as (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)
options: sorrowful and nostalgic
cynical
hopeful and appreciative
alarmist
questions.explanation: Calling it 'an encouraging sign' and praising 'thoughtful adaptation' shows approval and hope, not sorrow or alarm.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the best title for the passage? (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)
options: Power Looms Defeat the Handloom
Rice Farming in Telangana
Designers Reject Traditional Textiles
Threads of Survival: How Pochampally Ikat Adapts
questions.explanation: The passage is about a traditional craft surviving by adapting. The first title says so; the others contradict or ignore the text.

questions.questionText: The central message of the passage is that (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)
options: UPI is convenient and widely adopted, but must stay reliable and accessible for vulnerable users.
UPI has failed and should be replaced by cash.
UPI works only for people who live in big cities.
Older people should be forbidden from handling payments.
questions.explanation: The passage praises UPI's reach, then raises concerns about outages and elderly users, and ends with a standard for serving everyone. Option one reflects this balance.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)
options: The government has withdrawn cash from circulation.
Reliance on digital payments has made small shops vulnerable to network failures.
UPI charges heavy fees from all users.
Elderly people prefer smartphones to cash.
questions.explanation: Shopkeepers lose sales when networks fail because customers no longer carry cash, so dependence on digital payment creates vulnerability. The other options are not in the passage; indeed UPI is said to be free for most users.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'fallback' (in 'cash should remain available as a fallback') means (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)
options: a penalty for late payment
a type of discount
an alternative to use if the main option fails
a final instalment
questions.explanation: Cash is proposed for when the digital network is down. A fallback is a reserve option for when the main one fails.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards UPI is best described as (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)
options: uncritically enthusiastic
hostile
bewildered
appreciative yet cautious
questions.explanation: The author credits UPI's success and also lists practical worries and ends with a demand for inclusiveness. That blend is appreciative yet cautious.

questions.questionText: The most suitable title for the passage is (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)
options: UPI: Convenience That Must Reach Everyone
Banks Begin Charging for Digital Payments
How Flower Sellers Became Wealthy
Why Cash Should Be Banned
questions.explanation: The passage balances UPI's convenience with the need to include those with weak connections or low confidence. The first title does that; the other options misrepresent the content.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)
options: Shrimp farming is banned throughout the Sundarbans.
Mangrove clearing continues because it brings quick private profit despite long-term collective risk.
Mangroves grow best on land cleared for ponds.
Ghoramara is protected by dense mangroves.
questions.explanation: The passage says shrimp farming 'pays quickly' while mangrove benefits 'arrive slowly and are shared by everyone', explaining continued clearing. Nothing supports a ban, and Ghoramara is described as being swallowed by the sea.

questions.questionText: The word 'swallowing' in 'swallowing islands such as Ghoramara' most nearly means (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)
options: eating
storing safely
submerging gradually
blocking off
questions.explanation: The islands are lost to rising sea level and families must leave, so the sea is covering them. 'Swallowing' is used figuratively to mean engulfing or submerging.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards the conservation effort is best described as (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)
options: resigned and hopeless
humorous
accusatory towards villagers
concerned yet constructive
questions.explanation: The author warns about funding and sea-level rise but praises the partnership approach 'rather than offenders'. That is concern with a constructive bent, not hopelessness or blame.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a forecast rather than an established fact? (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)
options: If planting is abandoned, the sea will reclaim what villagers began to restore.
Villages shielded by dense mangroves suffered less damage in Cyclone Amphan.
Rising sea levels are swallowing islands such as Ghoramara.
Conservation groups offer villagers paid work to plant saplings.
questions.explanation: The other statements describe events or practices that have occurred. The first describes what will happen in a future situation and cannot be verified as fact now.

questions.questionText: The best title for the passage is (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)
options: Shrimp Farming and Its Profits
Mangroves: The Sundarbans' Living Shield
A History of Bengal Cyclones
Why Islands Should Be Abandoned
questions.explanation: The passage presents mangroves as a protective barrier and discusses efforts to keep it. The first title says that; the others cover side topics or reverse the message.

questions.questionText: The passage mainly argues that (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)
options: libraries are valuable only for retired readers of newspapers.
flyovers should be replaced by libraries in every city.
libraries can serve as lively community spaces and deserve public support.
young people prefer libraries because of the books alone.
questions.explanation: The passage gives examples of libraries serving young people and makes a case against cutting their funds. The first option summarises that; the others exaggerate or reverse the text.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'trimmed' (in 'to be trimmed when money is short') means (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)
options: decorated
praised
expanded
reduced
questions.explanation: When money is scarce, officials cut spending on libraries, so 'trimmed' means cut down or reduced.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards libraries is best described as (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)
options: earnestly supportive
mockingly critical
neutral and unconcerned
regretful and nostalgic
questions.explanation: The author praises the new services and criticises officials who undervalue libraries ('mistakes their purpose'). That is committed support, not neutrality.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion expressed in the passage? (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)
options: The reading room of a Pune library is filled by six every morning.
A library that opens opportunities does more for a city than another flyover.
A Kozhikode district library keeps its doors open until late in the evening.
Librarians report that the number of young members has doubled.
questions.explanation: The other three are reports of practices or figures that can be checked. Comparing a library's worth with a flyover's is a value judgement.

questions.questionText: The most suitable title for the passage is (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)
options: The Decline of Newspaper Reading
Coding Classes in Kozhikode
Libraries as Community Spaces, Not Just Quiet Rooms
Why Flyovers Cost So Much
questions.explanation: The passage shows libraries changing from quiet reading rooms to community spaces. The first title captures this; the others are narrower or irrelevant.

questions.questionText: The main point of the passage is that (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)
options: Indians are naturally more disciplined than other people.
the Delhi Metro has failed to serve the middle class.
fines are more effective than clear signs or frequent trains.
the Delhi Metro shows that public behaviour improves when the system is well designed and enforced.
questions.explanation: The passage rejects the old predictions, credits design and enforcement, and treats later criticism as being about reach and not about behaviour. The first option states this; the others invent claims or rank factors the passage does not.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the early predictions about commuter behaviour (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)
options: underestimated the influence of system design.
were based on careful studies of Metro users.
were confirmed by later events.
applied only to Kochi and Lucknow.
questions.explanation: Planners credit good behaviour to design, not to special virtue, and say the predictions 'look wrong'. So the predictions had underrated how much design shapes conduct.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage is best described as (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)
options: cynical
analytical and approving
fearful
satirical
questions.explanation: The author explains why the Metro works and praises its lessons, while granting that criticisms are fair. That is analytical and approving.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion? (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)
options: The Delhi Metro opened its first line in 2002.
Stations in Kochi and Lucknow were planned with wide stairways.
The complaints about limited reach and poor last-mile connectivity are fair.
Security checks are routine in the Metro.
questions.explanation: The first statement judges whether the complaints are fair, which depends on viewpoint. The other three describe dates, design features and practices that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage? (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)
options: The Failure of Public Transport in India
Why Indians Dislike Queues
Women's Coaches and Their Critics
Good Design, Good Behaviour: The Metro Lesson
questions.explanation: The passage argues that design and enforcement changed public conduct on the Metro. The first title expresses that central lesson; the others reverse or narrow it.

questions.questionText: The passage is primarily about (Passage: Chennai and Chess)
options: Chennai's rise in chess, which has produced success but also carries the risk of burnout in young players.
the history of chess tournaments organised abroad.
the failure of online classes to teach chess.
the need to ban children from tournaments altogether.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the causes of Chennai's success and then the warning about pressure. The first option covers both. The others are unsupported.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Chennai and Chess)
options: Online classes have reduced children's interest in chess.
Many Chennai players first learn chess informally at home before any academy training.
All grandmasters from the city eventually burn out.
The state government opposed hosting international tournaments.
questions.explanation: The passage describes a child learning from an uncle on the verandah 'long before joining a formal academy'. It does not say online classes reduced interest or that every grandmaster burns out.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'prodigies' means (Passage: Chennai and Chess)
options: beginners of average skill
coaches in schools
exceptionally talented young people
tournament organisers
questions.explanation: The state funded a few young 'prodigies' and the following sentence mentions teenagers earning grandmaster titles. A prodigy is a young person with outstanding ability.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion? (Passage: Chennai and Chess)
options: Several teenagers from Chennai have earned grandmaster titles.
The state government hosted an international tournament.
Coaches began offering group classes in schools.
The game's joy is meant to sustain a player, not merely the title.
questions.explanation: The other statements are events that can be verified. What chess is 'meant' to do for a player is a belief about values, which makes it an opinion.

questions.questionText: The best title for the passage is (Passage: Chennai and Chess)
options: Chennai's Chess Boom: Talent, Support and the Risk of Burnout
Why Chess Should Replace Cricket
The Verandah Games of Mumbai
Online Classes and Their Failures
questions.explanation: The passage covers Chennai's success factors and the risk of early pressure. The first title includes both; the others cover things the passage never says.

questions.questionText: The main idea of the passage is that (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)
options: solar power is impossible in cities with crowded rooftops.
Modhera's solar success, though small in scale, shows that ordinary communities can run renewable energy.
Modhera's temple is the main reason for its solar plant.
batteries are the only important part of solar systems.
questions.explanation: The passage's point is what Modhera 'shows': local people can manage solar power. It admits larger towns will find it harder, but does not say it is impossible.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)
options: No town can ever adopt solar power.
Households in Modhera now pay more for electricity.
Copying the Modhera model in dense cities will face practical obstacles such as divided ownership.
Batteries are unnecessary in solar systems.
questions.explanation: The passage says larger towns will find it harder because of crowded rooftops and divided ownership, so obstacles are expected, though 'may well be able' keeps the door open. The other options contradict the text.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'surplus' means (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)
options: a shortage
the cost of installation
a type of battery
the amount left over beyond what is needed
questions.explanation: Batteries store the 'surplus' for use after sunset, so it is electricity produced beyond immediate use. A surplus is an excess.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards Modhera's example is best described as (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)
options: optimistic and encouraging
disapproving
anxious
indifferent
questions.explanation: The author highlights bill savings and local competence, and ends with a hopeful extension to cities. The tone is optimistic.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage? (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)
options: The History of Sun Temples in Gujarat
Modhera: A Village That Runs on the Sun
Why Solar Power Fails in Cities
Rising Electricity Bills in Gujarat
questions.explanation: The passage reports Modhera's solar transformation and what it demonstrates. The first title matches; the others are unrelated or contradict the text.
